questions.stem: Which of these is written as a testable hypothesis about the human body?
options: Caffeine is bad for people and should not be sold to students
Some people prefer drinking coffee to drinking tea in the morning
Heart rate is an interesting thing to measure in a laboratory
If caffeine intake increases, then resting heart rate will increase
questions.explanation: A hypothesis proposes a relationship between an independent and a dependent variable that can be tested by measurement. Value judgements and preferences cannot be tested this way.

questions.stem: Students test whether the temperature of the water affects how long it takes to dissolve a tablet of a digestive enzyme supplement. What is the independent variable?
options: The time taken for the tablet to dissolve
The volume of water in each beaker
The brand of enzyme supplement used
The temperature of the water
questions.explanation: The independent variable is the one the investigator deliberately changes, here the water temperature. The time taken is the dependent variable, and volume and brand should be controlled.

questions.stem: A student investigates the effect of exercise intensity on breathing rate. Which variable should be controlled?
options: The breathing rate after exercise
The intensity of exercise performed
The conclusion drawn from the results
How long each person exercises
questions.explanation: Controlled variables are kept the same so that any change in the dependent variable (breathing rate) can be attributed to the independent variable (intensity). Duration of exercise would otherwise also affect breathing.

questions.stem: In a trial of a new pain relief cream, one group receives the cream and another receives an identical cream with no active ingredient. What is the purpose of the second group?
options: It lets participants choose which cream they would rather use
It tests whether the active ingredient is safe at a higher dose
It is a control showing what happens without the active ingredient
It doubles the sample size so that the results become more precise
questions.explanation: A control group is treated identically except for the factor being tested, so any difference can be attributed to the active ingredient. The identical inactive cream is a placebo.

questions.stem: In a double-blind drug trial, neither the participants nor the researchers recording results know who received the drug. Why is this design used?
options: It ensures every participant receives the drug at some stage of the trial
It removes the need for a control group because no one knows the groups
It guarantees that the results will support the original hypothesis
It reduces bias from the expectations of participants and researchers
questions.explanation: If participants know they have the drug, expectation can change how they feel (the placebo effect); if researchers know, they may unconsciously record results differently. Blinding guards against both.

questions.stem: Which prediction follows from the hypothesis that regular aerobic training lowers resting heart rate?
options: After eight weeks of training, participants will all have identical resting heart rates
After eight weeks of training, participants' resting heart rates will be lower than before
After eight weeks of training, participants will report enjoying aerobic exercise more
After eight weeks without training, participants' heart rates will be impossible to measure
questions.explanation: A prediction states the specific, measurable result expected if the hypothesis is correct. Enjoyment is not the variable in the hypothesis.

questions.stem: What does it mean for an experiment to be valid?
options: It produces results that agree with the hypothesis being tested
It uses the most expensive and modern equipment available
It tests what it claims to test, with other variables controlled
It gives the same results each time it is repeated by the same person
questions.explanation: Validity is about whether the method measures what it is meant to measure, which requires a fair test with controlled variables. Getting consistent results on repetition is reliability.

questions.stem: How can a student make their measurements of reaction time more reliable?
options: Repeat the test for each person and calculate a mean
Test only one person once, so that there is no variation
Change several variables at once to see more effects
Record only the fastest result for each person tested
questions.explanation: Repeating trials and averaging reduces the effect of random variation, and consistent repeated results show reliability. Keeping only the fastest result would bias the data.

questions.stem: Four readings of a person's body temperature are 36.1, 36.2, 36.1 and 36.2 °C, but the thermometer is known to read 1.0 °C too low. How would you describe these readings?
options: Precise but not accurate
Accurate but not precise
Both accurate and precise
Neither accurate nor precise
questions.explanation: The readings are close to each other, so they are precise, but they are all about 1 °C below the true value, so they are not accurate. A systematic error causes this pattern.

questions.stem: A set of blood pressure readings varies widely, but their mean is very close to the true value. Which description fits?
options: Precise but not accurate
Both precise and accurate
Valid but completely unreliable
Accurate on average but not precise
questions.explanation: Accuracy is closeness to the true value, which the mean achieves; precision is closeness of readings to each other, which these lack. Wide scatter usually indicates random error.

questions.stem: A balance has not been zeroed and adds 0.5 g to every mass recorded. What type of error is this?
options: Random error
Human mistake in reading only
Sampling error
Systematic error
questions.explanation: A systematic error shifts every reading by the same amount in the same direction, affecting accuracy; repeating the measurement does not remove it. Random errors vary unpredictably.

questions.stem: Students time pulse counts with a stopwatch, starting and stopping it by hand. Which type of error does this mainly introduce?
options: No error, because a stopwatch is a digital instrument
Parallax error, because the display is read at an angle
Random error, because reaction time varies from trial to trial
Systematic error, because the stopwatch adds a fixed amount each time
questions.explanation: Human reaction times vary unpredictably, so timings scatter around the true value. Repeating and averaging reduces the effect of this random error.

questions.stem: How do random and systematic errors differ in how they can be reduced?
options: Neither can be reduced, so they are simply reported in the conclusion of the report
Random error is reduced by repeats and averaging; systematic error needs recalibration
Systematic error is reduced by repeats and averaging; random error needs recalibration of instruments
Both are removed completely by increasing the number of repeats in the investigation
questions.explanation: Averaging many readings cancels out random scatter but leaves a consistent offset unchanged. Systematic errors are fixed by calibrating instruments or improving technique.

questions.stem: A group measures lung capacity in five volunteers and finds a strong link with height. Why should their conclusion be treated with caution?
options: Five volunteers is too many, which makes the trend harder to see
The sample is very small, so the pattern may not apply to the wider population
Lung capacity cannot be measured in living people, so the data must be invalid
A strong link always proves that height directly causes lung capacity
questions.explanation: Small samples are easily affected by chance and by unusual individuals, so findings may not be representative. Larger samples give more confidence in a trend.

questions.stem: One heart rate reading is far higher than all others taken under the same conditions. What should the student do?
options: Use only that reading because unusual results are the most important
Change the hypothesis so that it matches the unusual reading
Look for a cause, repeat it if possible, and report any exclusion
Delete it without comment so the graph looks neater and more convincing
questions.explanation: An outlier may come from a mistake or a real effect, so it should be investigated and repeated; any reading left out of calculations must be reported and justified.

questions.stem: Five students' resting pulse rates (beats per minute) are 64, 70, 72, 70 and 84. What is the mean?
questions.explanation: The mean is the sum divided by the number of values: (64 + 70 + 72 + 70 + 84) / 5 = 360 / 5 = 72. 70 is the median and the mode, and 20 is the range.

questions.stem: For the pulse rates 64, 70, 72, 70 and 84, what is the median?
questions.explanation: Ordered, the values are 64, 70, 70, 72, 84, so the middle value is 70. The median is less affected than the mean by an extreme value such as 84.

questions.stem: For the pulse rates 64, 70, 72, 70 and 84, what is the range, and what does it show?
options: 70; the middle value of the data
84; the highest possible pulse rate
20; how spread out the data are
72; the typical value of the data
questions.explanation: The range is the highest value minus the lowest: 84 − 64 = 20. It indicates the spread of the data, while the mean and median indicate a central value.

questions.stem: A data set of recovery times includes one patient who took far longer than the others. Why might the median be a better summary than the mean?
options: The median is not pulled towards an extreme value
The median always gives a larger value than the mean
The median uses every value equally in its calculation
The median can only be calculated when there are no outliers
questions.explanation: One extreme value raises the mean noticeably, while the median depends only on the middle of the ordered data. Using every value in the calculation is a property of the mean.

questions.stem: Students record the number of people with each ABO blood group in their class. Which graph is most appropriate?
options: A scatter graph with a trend line
A pie chart of the mean values
A bar graph
A line graph
questions.explanation: Blood group is a categorical variable, so separate bars for each group suit the data. Line graphs are for continuous independent variables such as time or temperature.

questions.stem: Enzyme activity is measured at temperatures from 10 °C to 60 °C. Which graph should be drawn, and on which axes?
options: A pie chart showing the proportion of activity at each temperature
A line graph with temperature on the x-axis and enzyme activity on the y-axis
A line graph with enzyme activity on the x-axis and temperature on the y-axis
A bar graph with a separate bar for each colour of the reaction mixture
questions.explanation: Temperature is a continuous independent variable, so a line graph is used with it on the horizontal axis and the dependent variable on the vertical axis.

questions.stem: A survey finds that people who sleep fewer hours tend to have higher body mass. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Weight gain definitely causes short sleep, because heavier people sleep less
There is no relationship, because surveys can never provide scientific evidence
There is a correlation, but it does not show that short sleep causes weight gain
Short sleep definitely causes weight gain, because the two variables are linked
questions.explanation: A correlation shows that two variables change together, but a third factor such as diet or stress could affect both. A controlled experiment is needed to test cause and effect.

questions.stem: Two carriers of a recessive disorder plan a family. What is the probability that their first two children are both affected?
questions.explanation: Each child has a 1/4 chance and the events are independent, so the probability of both is 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16. Adding the probabilities would give an incorrect 1/2.

questions.stem: Before taking part in a study measuring their blood glucose, volunteers are told the purpose, procedures and risks and agree in writing. What is this called?
options: Informed consent
Peer review
Random sampling
Risk assessment plan
questions.explanation: Informed consent means participants understand what is involved and agree voluntarily. They must also be free to withdraw at any time without penalty.

questions.stem: A study records participants' heights, masses and medical histories. Which practice protects their confidentiality?
options: Storing data with codes instead of names and limiting who can see it
Publishing each participant's name beside their results in the report
Sharing the results on social media so that participants can find them
Asking participants to swap data sheets so others can check them
questions.explanation: De-identifying data and restricting access ensures personal health information cannot be linked to individuals. Confidentiality is a core principle of research ethics.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of a risk assessment before an investigation?
options: To identify hazards and plan how to reduce the chance of harm
To predict the results so the hypothesis can be confirmed
To choose which data to leave out of the final report
To decide which students should write the conclusion
questions.explanation: A risk assessment lists hazards, such as sharp equipment, body fluids or overexertion during exercise, judges their risk and sets out precautions.

questions.stem: Students plan to compare heart rate recovery in volunteers. Which practice best follows both safety and ethical guidelines?
options: Ask every volunteer to exercise until exhaustion so the results show the largest effect
Include only volunteers with heart conditions so that the differences are easier to see
Use the same volunteer for every trial without asking, to keep the variables controlled
Screen volunteers for health conditions, let them stop any time, keep exercise moderate
questions.explanation: Screening identifies people for whom exercise is risky, moderate exercise limits harm, and the right to withdraw respects participants. Pushing to exhaustion or targeting at-risk people breaches both principles.

questions.stem: When animals must be used in biomedical research, which principle guides their ethical use?
options: Use animals freely, because animals are not covered by any rules or guidelines in Australia
Replace animals where possible, reduce numbers used and refine methods to limit suffering
Use as many animals as possible so that the results become more reliable and convincing
Use animals only when the research has already been completed successfully on humans
questions.explanation: The principles of replacement, reduction and refinement guide animal research, and Australian research using animals must be approved by an animal ethics committee.

questions.stem: A website claims that a herbal tablet 'boosts immunity', quoting three satisfied customers. Why is this weak evidence?
options: Herbal products cannot have any effects on the human body at all
Testimonials are not controlled data and may reflect bias or chance
Customers are not allowed to give opinions about health products
The claim would only be valid if more than three tablets were taken
questions.explanation: Anecdotes lack controls, blinding and adequate sample size, and the seller has a financial interest. A controlled trial would be needed to test the claim.

questions.stem: Why is peer review important before a study is published in a scientific journal?
options: Independent experts check the methods, analysis and conclusions
It guarantees that the study's conclusions are correct for all time
It allows the authors to change their data after seeing other results
It ensures that the study is reported in newspapers before journals
questions.explanation: Peer review lets other scientists scrutinise a study and identify flaws before publication. It improves reliability but does not make conclusions final; later evidence can overturn them.

questions.stem: A study showing that a sports drink improves performance was funded by the drink's manufacturer. How should a reader respond?
options: Consider possible bias and look for independent replication of the result
Reject the result completely, because funded studies are always fraudulent
Accept the result without question, because the company knows its product best
Ignore the methods and focus only on the advertising that reports the study
questions.explanation: A conflict of interest does not prove a study wrong, but it is a reason to check the methods closely and to seek independent replication before accepting the claim.

questions.stem: A student uses a balloon in a bell jar, with a rubber sheet as the diaphragm, to model breathing. What is a limitation of this model?
options: It shows that the lungs follow changes in the volume of the chest
It does not show the movement of the ribs and intercostal muscles
It shows that air moves in when the volume inside the jar increases
It shows that pulling the rubber sheet down lowers the pressure inside
questions.explanation: Models simplify reality: a rigid bell jar cannot show the rib cage moving up and out. The other statements describe what the model does represent well.

questions.stem: Which representation would best show the number and structure of chromosomes in a person's cells?
options: A pedigree chart
A Punnett square
A line graph
A karyotype
questions.explanation: A karyotype is an ordered image of a cell's chromosomes, used to identify conditions such as trisomy 21. Pedigrees show inheritance through families and Punnett squares show possible offspring of a cross.

questions.stem: In which section of a scientific report should the results be interpreted and the limitations of the method be evaluated?
options: The title
The discussion
The aim
The materials list
questions.explanation: The discussion explains what the results mean, links them to biological concepts, evaluates errors and limitations and suggests improvements. The conclusion then answers the aim briefly.

questions.stem: Which of these is qualitative data?
options: The glucose concentration of a urine sample
The colour of a urine sample
The volume of a urine sample
The pH of a urine sample
questions.explanation: Qualitative data describe qualities that are not measured as numbers, such as colour. Volume, pH and concentration are measured numerically, so they are quantitative.

questions.stem: A student uses published national data on blood donation rather than collecting data themselves. What type of data is this?
options: Control data
Secondary data
Primary data
Qualitative data only
questions.explanation: Secondary data were collected by someone else, here a national agency; primary data are collected first-hand by the investigator. Secondary sources should be checked for reliability.

questions.stem: A student's experiment supports the hypothesis that a warm-up improves flexibility. Which statement is the best conclusion?
options: The hypothesis must be rejected because supporting results are always suspicious
The results show the hypothesis cannot be tested by experiment or observation
The results support the hypothesis for this sample; more trials would strengthen this
The results prove the hypothesis is true for all people in every circumstance
questions.explanation: Results can support a hypothesis but cannot prove it absolutely, especially from one sample. A sound conclusion states what the evidence shows and acknowledges its limits.
